Punishment, Deterrents and Rehabilitation

Earlier lessons in this unit looked at theories that try to explain why people offend — Social Learning Theory and Eysenck’s Criminal Personality Theory. This lesson looks at what happens next: how the criminal justice system tries to stop offending happening again. There are two broad approaches. One tries to change the offender from the inside — rehabilitation. The other tries to stop offending through consequences — punishment and deterrents.

Key Fact

The specification names two specific approaches to rehabilitation: restorative justice and the use of positive role models. Both aim to reduce criminal/anti-social behaviour and increase pro-social behaviour, rather than simply punishing the offender.

What Is Rehabilitation?

Rehabilitation focuses on changing the offender, not just punishing the act. The goal is to reduce criminal/anti-social behaviour and increase pro-social behaviour — behaviour that benefits other people rather than harms them.

One rehabilitation method is the use of positive role models, such as mentors or reformed ex-offenders. This links directly to Social Learning Theory from earlier in the unit: if people learn criminal behaviour by identifying with and imitating models, then exposing them to models who show pro-social behaviour should encourage them to imitate that instead. Seeing a positive role model rewarded for pro-social choices works as vicarious reinforcement in reverse.

Restorative justice brings the offender into direct contact with the victim, or hears from them, so the offender has to face the real human impact of what they did. It often includes reparation — repairing damage or offering an apology.

Restorative justice aims to build empathy and accountability in the offender and gives the victim a voice in the process. It is often used alongside, or instead of, a custodial sentence for less serious or first-time offences, rather than for the most serious violent crimes.

Punishment and Deterrents

A deterrent works by making offending unattractive: the unpleasant consequence should put the offender off reoffending (individual deterrence) and put other people off offending in the first place (general deterrence). Prisons are the most severe deterrent used in the UK justice system.

Prisons remove the offender from society, protecting the public in the short term. The loss of liberty is meant to deter both the individual and others. However, prisons are criticised for high reoffending rates: contact with other offenders inside prison can expose someone to more criminal role models rather than fewer, and many prisons offer limited access to rehabilitation programmes.

Key Fact

The specification names three types of punishment/deterrent: prisons, community sentences and fines. Each aims to reduce offending in a different way, and each has strengths and weaknesses that examiners expect you to weigh up.

Community Sentences and Fines

A community sentence might include unpaid work, an electronically monitored curfew, or a treatment programme. Because the offender stays in the community, they can often keep their job and family ties while still facing a consequence for their crime.

A fine is a financial penalty, usually set in proportion to both the offence and the offender’s income. Fines are quick and cheap to administer, but critics argue they do not address the underlying causes of offending, and that a fine easily afforded by a wealthier offender has little deterrent value.

Prisons incapacitate offenders and give a severe consequence for serious or violent crime, but they are expensive to run and exposure to other offenders can increase reoffending rather than reduce it, giving prisoners little chance to practise pro-social behaviour.

Community sentences are cheaper and keep offenders connected to work, family and rehabilitation support, which can lower reoffending for many lower-level offences. However, some victims and the public see them as too lenient, and they rely on the offender actually complying with the conditions set.

Evaluating What Works

Rehabilitation approaches assume that criminal behaviour is learned and can be relearned — this fits the nurture side of the nature/nurture debate and connects to Social Learning Theory. Punishment and deterrence approaches assume the offender has free will and will choose not to reoffend once faced with unpleasant consequences — connecting to the free will/determinism debate.

No single approach works for every offender or every crime. An offender whose behaviour is better explained by Eysenck’s biological personality theory — high psychoticism or neuroticism, for example — may need a different intervention than an offender who learned criminal behaviour from role models. Most modern justice systems combine punishment, deterrents and rehabilitation rather than relying on just one.

Doing Research: Experiments, Interviews, Questionnaires and Observations

Once a researcher has written a hypothesis and identified their variables, they must decide how to actually collect data. OCR groups this stage as ‘doing research’ and covers three broad approaches: experiments, self-report methods such as interviews and questionnaires, and observations. Each approach has its own strengths and weaknesses, and each suits a different kind of research question.

Key Fact

The three types of experiment are laboratory, field and natural. A laboratory experiment gives the researcher the most control over variables but the least realistic behaviour. A field experiment trades some control for a real-world setting. A natural experiment studies an independent variable that occurs naturally, without any manipulation by the researcher.

Laboratory, Field and Natural Experiments

All three types of experiment involve measuring the effect of an independent variable on a dependent variable. They differ mainly in where they take place and how much control the researcher has over the environment.

A laboratory experiment takes place in a specially controlled setting, such as a university lab. The researcher can control lighting, noise, timing and the exact stimuli each participant sees. Strength: high control makes results easier to replicate and more clearly linked to the IV. Weakness: the artificial setting can reduce how naturally participants behave, so results may not reflect everyday life.

A field experiment takes place in a real-world setting, such as a school or shop, while the researcher still deliberately manipulates the independent variable. Strength: participants behave more naturally because they are in a familiar environment. Weakness: the researcher has less control over other variables that might affect the results.

A natural experiment studies an independent variable that would have changed anyway, such as comparing behaviour before and after a change in law. Strength: it allows psychologists to study variables that would be unethical or impossible to manipulate directly. Weakness: participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions, so it is harder to be sure the IV caused any difference found.

Interviews

A structured interview asks every participant the same fixed questions, in the same order. Strength: because every participant answers identical questions, the interview is easy to repeat and answers are simple to compare. Weakness: the interviewer cannot follow up on an interesting or unexpected answer, so some detail may be lost.

An unstructured interview has no fixed questions. It works more like a guided conversation, with the interviewer free to ask follow-up questions based on what the participant says. Strength: it can produce rich, detailed qualitative data and can explore topics a structured interview would miss. Weakness: interviews are hard to repeat in exactly the same way, and the interviewer’s own views may unintentionally influence the questions asked.

Questionnaires: Open, Closed and Rating-Scale Questions

Closed questions give the respondent a fixed set of possible answers, such as ‘yes/no’ or a list of options. They produce quantitative data that is quick to score and easy to compare across large numbers of respondents.

Open questions have no fixed answers — the respondent replies in their own words. They produce qualitative data with more depth and detail, but the answers are harder to analyse and compare because every respondent may word their answer differently.

A rating scale asks respondents to indicate the strength of an opinion on a numbered range, for example from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). This turns an attitude into a number, so it can be added up and compared statistically, though respondents may avoid the extreme ends of the scale.

Key Fact

Closed questions and rating scales produce quantitative data that is quick to analyse; open questions produce qualitative data with more depth but less ease of comparison. Choosing between them depends on whether the researcher wants breadth (many respondents, simple answers) or depth (fewer respondents, detailed answers).

Observations

Observations involve watching and recording behaviour rather than asking about it. OCR describes observations using three separate pairs of contrasting terms: the setting (naturalistic or controlled), whether participants know they are being watched (overt or covert), and whether the researcher takes part (participant or non-participant). A single study combines one option from each pair.

A naturalistic observation watches behaviour in its normal, everyday setting, with no interference from the researcher. Strength: high ecological validity because behaviour is unaffected by the research process. A controlled observation takes place in a setting where the researcher has altered some conditions, such as observing children through a one-way mirror in a set-up room. Strength: easier to control extraneous variables and to repeat the observation exactly. Weakness: the artificial setting may reduce how naturally participants behave.

In an overt observation, participants know they are being watched, which respects their right to consent but can cause them to change their behaviour because they are aware of being observed. In a covert observation, participants do not know they are being watched, so behaviour is more natural, but this raises ethical concerns about consent and privacy.

In participant observation, the researcher joins in with the activity or group being studied, which can give unique insight into a group’s behaviour from the inside. In non-participant observation, the researcher stays separate and simply watches, which keeps their judgement more objective but may miss detail only visible from within the group.

Key Fact

Observations vary along three independent dimensions — setting (naturalistic or controlled), participant awareness (overt or covert), and researcher involvement (participant or non-participant). A single study can combine any of these, for example a covert, non-participant, naturalistic observation of shoppers in a supermarket.

Choosing the Right Method

The right choice always depends on the research question. A topic needing strict control, such as testing a precise cognitive theory, suits a laboratory experiment. A topic needing natural behaviour, such as helping behaviour in public, suits a field experiment or naturalistic observation. A topic needing personal detail and explanation, such as someone’s experience of a mental health problem, suits an unstructured interview or open questions. In every case, examiners want you to name the specific method precisely and explain why it fits the scenario given, not just describe it in general terms.

Turning Data into Meaning

Once a psychologist has collected data, they need to summarise it so that patterns become visible. Descriptive statistics, tables and graphs are the tools that do this. They appear throughout both components — you might be asked to calculate a mean in a Criminal Psychology question just as easily as in the Research Methods section, so these skills need to be secure across the whole course.

Measures of Central Tendency

Measures of central tendency summarise the ‘average’ of a dataset, but the three measures — mean, median and mode — each give a different picture of what is typical.

The mean is found by adding every value together and dividing by the number of values. If five participants scored 7, 8, 6, 9 and 5 on a memory test, the mean is $$\frac{7+8+6+9+5}{5} = \frac{35}{5} = 7$$. The mean uses every score, but a single outlier can pull it up or down.

The median is the middle value once the data is placed in order from lowest to highest. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle scores. Because it ignores extreme scores, the median is often more useful than the mean when a dataset contains outliers.

The mode is the value that appears most often. It is the only measure that works with categorical data, such as the most common favourite colour in a sample. When data has been grouped into ranges, psychologists refer to the modal class — the group with the highest frequency — rather than a single modal value.

Range

The range shows how spread out a dataset is. It is calculated as the highest value minus the lowest. For the scores 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, the range is \(9 - 5 = 4\). A large range means participants performed very differently from each other; a small range means their scores were similar. Like the mean, the range is sensitive to outliers.

Key Fact

Mean = total ÷ number of values. Median = middle value in ordered data. Mode = most frequent value (or modal class for grouped data). Range = highest minus lowest. Mean and range are both distorted by outliers; the median is not.

Maths Skills: Ratios, Fractions, Percentages and Standard Form

OCR expects you to use basic maths confidently, not just recall it. A ratio compares quantities directly — for example, if 15 out of 20 participants conformed, the ratio of conforming to non-conforming participants is 15:5, which simplifies to 3:1. The same result could be expressed as a fraction (\(\frac{3}{4}\) conformed) or a percentage (75% conformed). Being able to move between these forms — fraction, decimal, percentage — is a skill examiners test directly.

Very large or very small numbers, such as a count of neurons involved in a brain process, are sometimes written in standard form, for example \(3.2 \times 10^4\). When rounding a calculated answer, give it to an appropriate number of significant figures — usually two or three, unless the question tells you otherwise. Always show your working before giving a final rounded answer.

Key Fact

A ratio compares two quantities directly (e.g. 3:1). The same relationship can be shown as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage. Standard form writes very large or small numbers as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

Displaying Data: Tables, Charts and Graphs

Frequency tables record how many times each value, or range of values, occurs, and are usually the first step before drawing a chart. A bar chart displays discrete or categorical data as separate bars with gaps between them — for example, the number of participants in each experimental condition. A pie chart shows how a total is divided into proportions, useful for displaying percentages of a sample who hold different views.

A histogram looks like a bar chart but is used for continuous data, such as ages or reaction times grouped into ranges — the bars touch because the underlying scale has no gaps. A line graph plots change over time, such as the number of hours slept across a week. A scatter diagram plots pairs of values as points to reveal whether a correlation exists between two co-variables, such as hours of revision and exam score.

Many psychological variables, when measured across a large population, form a normal distribution. Plotted as a graph, this produces a symmetrical bell-shaped curve. In a normal distribution, the mean, median and mode all sit at the same central point, and scores become rarer the further they are from that centre.

IQ scores and height are classic examples — most people score close to the average, with progressively fewer people at the extremes. The normal distribution matters because it gives psychologists a benchmark: a score close to the mean is typical, while a score in the extreme tail is unusual. Many statistical tests also assume the data being analysed is approximately normally distributed.

Reliability

Reliability asks whether a study or measure is consistent. Internal reliability checks whether a measure is consistent within itself — for example, whether different questions on the same questionnaire produce a consistent pattern of answers. External reliability checks whether a measure gives consistent results when repeated over time or in a different setting, such as a test-retest. Inter-rater reliability checks whether two or more observers scoring the same behaviour agree — high agreement increases confidence that the observation is measuring something real rather than personal judgement.

Validity

Validity asks whether a study genuinely measures what it claims to measure. Ecological validity concerns whether findings from an artificial setting, such as a laboratory, apply to everyday life. Population validity concerns whether findings from one sample can be generalised to the wider population the sample was meant to represent. Construct validity concerns whether a test genuinely measures the underlying psychological concept it is supposed to measure, rather than something else entirely.

Key Fact

Reliability: internal (consistent within the measure), external (consistent over time or settings), inter-rater (consistent between observers). Validity: ecological (applies to real life), population (generalises to the wider population), construct (measures the real underlying concept).
